questions.q: In Rust, what happens to a `String` value when the variable that owns it goes out of scope?
choices: It is moved onto the heap
It leaks unless you call free()
questions.why: Rust's ownership model drops a value and frees its memory at the end of its owner's scope. There is no garbage collector and no manual free.

questions.q: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{}", a);` — what does the compiler report?
choices: Warning: unused variable `b`, then prints hi
questions.why: Assigning a non-Copy value moves it; `a` is no longer valid. The fix is `a.clone()` or borrowing with `&a`.

questions.q: A function takes `&mut Vec<i32>`, creates `let it = v.iter();`, then calls `v.push(1)` and later uses `it`. What happens?
choices: Compiles cleanly: the borrow from `iter()` ends at the `push` call, before `it` is used again
Error: cannot borrow `*v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable by `it`
Error: `Vec<i32>` is not `Send`, so it cannot be iterated and mutated in one scope
Compiles, with a warning that `it` is an unused iterator because `push` invalidated it
questions.why: The immutable borrow from `iter()` lives as long as `it` is used. A `push` while it is alive conflicts. Non-lexical lifetimes only end the borrow after the last use of `it`.

questions.q: Why does `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` reject a call where `y` is a `String` created inside an inner block and the result is used after that block?
choices: Because a `String` created in an inner block cannot be coerced to `&str` outside that block
Because the returned reference's lifetime is tied to the shorter of the two input lifetimes
Because `'a` on a returned reference must be `'static` unless both inputs are string literals
Because the compiler picks the longer of the two input lifetimes and `x` outlives the block
questions.why: One lifetime parameter for both inputs means the output lives no longer than the shorter input. The inner-block `String` dies at the block end, so the result cannot outlive it.
